questions.question: Vaccines differ in what they carry. Some hold a germ that has been killed, some a live germ weakened until it causes little or no illness, and some only a single protein taken from a germ's outer coat. Each kind can protect a child against the real germ. What do all three kinds give the immune system?
questions.answer: A shape its own cells can learn to recognise
choices: A shape its own cells can learn to recognise
A general boost that strengthens every defence at once
Germ material that blocks the real germ's way into cells
Germ material that stays on to keep the defences busy
questions.context: The killed germ, the weakened germ and the lone protein all carry antigens, the molecular shapes that set off the body's own adaptive defences: B cells that fit the antigen multiply and many become plasma cells that make antibodies. The protection is aimed at that one germ rather than being a general boost, and it is the antibodies the body makes that later block the real germ from reaching cells; antibodies made in another body and given against a toxin are passive immunity, borrowed rather than learned.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches how the immune system answers an antigen and how a vaccine prepares it, a step beyond the sixth-grade idea that the body remembers a germ.

questions.question: A girl gets her first dose of a vaccine, and over the next week or two her blood slowly gains a modest amount of antibody against its antigen. Months later she gets a booster dose, and within a few days her antibody level climbs far higher than it did the first time. What makes the second response faster and larger?
questions.answer: Memory B cells formed after the first dose
choices: Memory B cells formed after the first dose
Antibodies still left over from the first dose
Antigen stored in her arm since the first dose
An immune system grown stronger with age
questions.context: The first time, the few B cells that fit the antigen must be found and multiplied, which takes days to weeks, and some of them stay behind as long-lived memory B cells. At the booster they turn quickly into antibody-making plasma cells, so the response comes in days and is many times larger, while the antibody from the first dose fades in the months between; that is why many vaccines, killed ones especially, are given more than once.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches the primary and secondary immune responses and the memory cells behind them, the reason vaccines are given in a series.

questions.question: Benjamin Jesty, a Dorset farmer, scratched matter from a cow with cowpox into the arms of his wife and two sons in 1774, with smallpox in his village. Edward Jenner, a country doctor, put cowpox matter into eight-year-old James Phipps in May 1796. Donald Hopkins, an American doctor and historian of smallpox, argued that the cowpox alone was not what made Jenner's work unique. What did Jenner do that Jesty had not?
questions.answer: Tested his cases with smallpox, then published them
choices: Tested his cases with smallpox, then published them
Explained how cowpox matter makes a body immune
Gave cowpox to a whole village during an epidemic
Persuaded Parliament to make vaccination compulsory
questions.context: On 1 July 1796 Jenner inoculated Phipps with matter from smallpox and no disease followed; he tested others the same way and paid to print the 23 cases of his Inquiry in 1798, while Jesty, though his sons later met smallpox unharmed, did not publicise his. Hopkins wrote that Jenner's unique contribution was that he 'then proved [by subsequent challenges] that they were immune to smallpox.' No one could yet explain how the protection worked, and England made infant vaccination compulsory only in 1853, thirty years after Jenner died.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks what turns a hunch into evidence, and Jenner's deliberate test and published cases are the classic contrast with an untested success.

questions.question: Search teams could find nearly every smallpox case by its rash, which looked unlike other illnesses, and the last natural case was in Somalia in 1977. The World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated in May 1980, the only human disease wiped out so far. Why could stopping the last cases end it for good?
questions.answer: No animal carried the virus, only people
choices: No animal carried the virus, only people
Every person alive had been vaccinated
Every lab had destroyed its virus stocks
Every case had been cured with a new drug
questions.context: Smallpox passes only from person to person, with no animal host and no part played by insects, so once no one anywhere was infected it had nowhere left to live; the easy-to-see rash and the lack of hidden carriers let teams find every outbreak. No proven drug for smallpox existed then, the campaign never vaccinated everyone, and stocks of the virus are still kept in two laboratories, at the CDC in the United States and at VECTOR in Russia.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches how infectious diseases spread between hosts, and smallpox shows why a disease with no animal host can be ended.

questions.question: William Foege, an American doctor in eastern Nigeria, faced a smallpox outbreak late in 1966 with too little vaccine to go round. Health officials then held that 80 to 100 percent of a population had to be vaccinated to stop smallpox. What did his teams do with the vaccine they had?
questions.answer: Vaccinated the people around each case
choices: Vaccinated the people around each case
Vaccinated every child under five
Vaccinated the people of the largest towns
Vaccinated the doctors and nurses
questions.context: Foege asked missionaries with radios to report every case they heard of, and his teams vaccinated the villages with cases, then the places the disease was likely to reach next along family and market routes; four weeks later the outbreak was over, before the shipment for mass vaccination had arrived. This surveillance and containment, or ring vaccination, became the method of the worldwide campaign; accounts of how small a share of people it took range from 7 or 8 percent to under half.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge a strategy by its evidence, and ring vaccination is the case where a targeted method beat the expected one.

questions.question: Cutter Laboratories of Berkeley, California, was licensed in 1955 to make Jonas Salk's new polio vaccine, which was meant to hold only killed virus. Some of Cutter's lots held live poliovirus, and in Paul Offit's 2005 account about 200 children were left with some paralysis and 10 died, though the lots had passed their safety tests. A congressional hearing looked into the cause in June 1955. Where did it lay most of the blame?
questions.answer: On too little checking by the federal laboratory
choices: On too little checking by the federal laboratory
On Cutter's workers, for faking their tests
On Jonas Salk, for a method that could never work
On the clinics, for storing the vaccine badly
questions.context: The hearing found the problem lay mainly in too little scrutiny by the federal Laboratory of Biologics Control, part of the National Institutes of Health: the required tests could not pick up a small amount of surviving virus, inspectors found nothing wrong with Cutter's methods, and the director of the National Institutes of Health had set aside Bernice Eddy's 1954 report of paralysed test monkeys. Later that year the laboratory became the Division of Biologics Standards and federal scientists began testing each lot before release; the killed-virus vaccine, made under the new checks, is the only polio vaccine the United States has used since 2000.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that a passed test is only as good as the test and the checking behind it, and the Cutter Incident is the standard case of a safety system that failed.

questions.question: Lawsuits over the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) shot rose from nine in the four years 1978 to 1981 to more than 200 by the mid-1980s, and by the end of 1985 only one American company still made the vaccine for pertussis, or whooping cough. Congress answered with the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act, signed in November 1986. What trade did the law make?
questions.answer: Makers faced fewer lawsuits; families could be paid without proving fault
choices: Makers faced fewer lawsuits; families could be paid without proving fault
Makers paid a set fine per injury; families gave up any claim to payment
Makers got federal grants to keep going; families got the shots for free
Makers were freed from all lawsuits; families could sue only their doctor
questions.context: A family that believes a covered vaccine caused an injury must first file with the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program before suing the maker or whoever gave the shot; a special master of the Court of Federal Claims decides without a jury and need find no one at fault, and the makers stay liable for faulty manufacture or poor warnings. The awards come from a trust fund filled by a tax of 75 cents on each dose for each disease it prevents, and about 5.4 billion dollars had been paid out by 2025.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science and society asks how institutions handle the risks of a technology, and the 1986 Act is the documented case for vaccines.

questions.question: Any person may send a report to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), run since 1990 by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration: a patient, a parent, a nurse or a vaccine maker. A boy breaks out in a rash two days after a shot, and his father files a report. What does that one report show by itself?
questions.answer: That the rash came after the shot
choices: That the rash came after the shot
That the shot caused the rash
That officials have confirmed the report
That the rash is a known side effect
questions.context: In the CDC's words, 'A VAERS report alone does not indicate whether a vaccine caused or contributed to an adverse event'; the rash might come from a virus, a food or anything else that week, and VAERS takes reports as they are sent, without first judging whether the vaccine was to blame, so some lack details or contain errors. That open door is what makes the system an early warning: in 1999 fifteen reports of a bowel blockage in babies after a new vaccine, RotaShield, led the CDC to urge a halt, and later studies confirmed the risk.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that one event following another is not proof that the first caused the second, and a passive reporting system is the plain case.

questions.question: Children in the early 1980s were routinely vaccinated against seven diseases; by 2013 the US schedule protected children up to age six against fourteen germs, with up to 24 vaccine doses by age two. An Institute of Medicine committee reviewed it that year and found no significant evidence that the schedule is not safe. What gap in the research did the same committee report?
questions.answer: The schedule as a whole had not been systematically studied
choices: The schedule as a whole had not been systematically studied
Its vaccines had not been checked for safety after licensing
Its vaccines had not been tested in children before licensing
The schedule had not been shown to make its diseases rarer
questions.context: The committee wrote that key elements of the entire schedule, the number, frequency, timing, order and age at which vaccines are given, 'have not been systematically examined in research studies', though each vaccine had been tested before licensing and watched afterward, and it credited the immunizations for the decline of the diseases they prevent; both halves of its finding are quoted on every side. It judged a randomised trial that left some children unvaccinated 'unethical and infeasible', and named the Vaccine Safety Datalink, linked health-plan records, as the best system for studying the schedule.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that honest science names what has not yet been studied, and the 2013 review states both its finding and its gap.

questions.question: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., calling for 'gold standard science', had his health department announce in May 2025 that every new vaccine would be tested against a placebo, an inert dummy shot, before approval. Steven Black, who helped run the 1990s trial of Prevnar, a pneumococcal vaccine for babies, said its control babies were given no dummy shot because of an ethical concern. What did the control babies get instead?
questions.answer: A vaccine against a different disease
choices: A vaccine against a different disease
An older vaccine against the same germ
Only their usual baby shots, nothing extra
The new vaccine, a year later
questions.context: The 37,868 babies were assigned at random, and the control half got an experimental vaccine against meningococcal disease, which Black said offered them a possible benefit, so the trial stayed double-blind with no dummy shot; on the wider question, Daniel Salmon of Johns Hopkins argues that when a disease already has a vaccine, a new one cannot ethically be tested against no vaccine at all. Christine Stabell Benn and Martin Kulldorff argued in a 2025 preprint that the double-blind, placebo-controlled trial is 'the gold standard of medical research', that few have been run for vaccines, and that much about vaccines is still unknown; they have proposed such trials of vaccines already in use, which Paul Offit called unethical, while Kennedy told senators, 'I'm not suggesting we go back and placebo test all childhood vaccines.' Any such trial needs the parents' informed consent, a rule that the Declaration of Helsinki of 1964 extended to consent by parents for children.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches what a control group is for, and an active control shows how a fair trial can run without leaving the controls unprotected.

questions.question: Ross Lazarus led a project at Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, paid for by the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, that built a system to find possible vaccine side effects in clinic records and report them to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Its final report, dated 2010, gave the reason the work was needed. What share of vaccine side effects did it say were being reported?
choices: Fewer than 1 in 100 side effects
About 1 in 10 side effects
About half of all side effects
Nearly all side effects, but late
questions.context: The report's background said that side effects of vaccines 'are common but underreported', with less than one percent reported; that figure is a reason given for the work, not a count the project made, and the team's own system flagged possible reactions after 2.6 percent of 1.4 million doses. Both cautions about VAERS stand together: anyone may file a report, and most problems are never reported.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to ask how a data set was collected and what it misses, and passive reporting is the standard example of undercounting.

dropped.question: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her son engrafted in the Ottoman Empire in 1718: matter from a smallpox sore was put into a small cut in his skin. Boston took up the practice in 1721, after Onesimus, an enslaved West African man, told the minister Cotton Mather of it. What did Edward Jenner's method, 75 years later, do away with?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: LEAD (2026-11-27): left to drop; the Jesty question (6940cc0a60) is kept, as it teaches what made Jenner's work science (tested and published). Its own stem is fixed: no cowpox and no death counts, engrafting is defined once, and all three lures are wrong on the record (Jenner still made small cuts, took his first matter from Sarah Nelmes's hand, and wrongly promised lifelong protection). Remaining problem: 6940cc0a60's stem says Jenner 'put cowpox matter into eight-year-old James Phipps' and that 'the cowpox alone was not what made Jenner's work unique'. That tells the player that Jenner's method used cowpox, not smallpox, which is this question's key. No one-phrase fix exists: the Jesty question needs cowpox in its stem. Keep one of the pair, or re-key this one (for example on Boylston's counts).
